query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A surface aluminizing treatment (e.g., pack cementation) on cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a thin, adherent, self-healing alumina (Al2O3) scale during high‐temperature exposure that significantly improves its oxidation resistance without altering the bulk microstructure, thereby preserving its reported room‐temperature tensile ductility and high‐temperature yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but with poor oxygen resistance due to unprotected reactive surfaces.
generation.intervention: Subject the cast alloy to a surface aluminizing process (e.g., pack cementation) that diffuses a small amount of aluminum into the outermost layer to enable formation of a continuous, adherent alumina scale during service.
generation.conditions: Testing in air at high temperatures (around 1000 °C) for extended exposure times (e.g., 100 hours) under typical strain rates (10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) with mechanical loading being unchanged from existing application conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanometrically thin, aluminide-modified surface layer that, upon high-temperature exposure, transforms into a protective Al2O3 scale.
generation.mechanism: The introduced aluminum diffuses into the surface and, at high temperatures in an oxidizing atmosphere, forms a slow-growing, thermodynamically stable, and adherent alumina scale. This layer acts as a barrier to oxygen ingress, thereby reducing bulk oxidation while leaving the alloy’s core microstructure—and its mechanical performance—essentially unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: Substantially reduced oxidation (i.e. lower mass gain and oxidation depth) relative to untreated HfNbTaTiZr during high-temperature exposure, while maintaining similar room-temperature tensile ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa) under the same mechanical-loading conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated, cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr which develops extensive oxidation during high-temperature exposure, compromising its service life.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective for high-temperature exposures around 1000 °C in air and under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1; its benefits may diminish outside these conditions or if the treated layer is too thick, which could potentially embrittle the surface.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal process parameters (aluminizing temperature, time, and aluminum concentration) must be calibrated to ensure the modified surface layer is protective yet thin enough not to alter the bulk mechanical properties; additionally, long-term cyclic oxidation behavior has not been fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set is subjected to the proposed surface aluminizing treatment via pack cementation, and the other is left untreated. Expose both sets to a high-temperature oxidizing environment at 1000 °C in air for 100 hours. After exposure, conduct oxidation weight-gain measurements (thermogravimetric analysis) and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (via SEM/EDS) to assess oxide scale formation. Additionally, perform room-temperature tensile tests and high-temperature yield strength tests (at 1000 °C, using strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1) on both sets to check for any changes in mechanical performance.
measurements: Oxidation weight gain per unit area
Thickness and continuity of the alumina scale (via SEM/EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxidation (e.g., less than a 20% reduction in weight gain or oxide thickness) compared to untreated samples, or if their room-temperature ductility decreases by more than 15% (or yield strength is compromised beyond the reported range) after treatment, then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are considered to be a new generation of high-temperature materials, because they have the advantages of both high-entropy alloys (HEAs) and refractory metals (RMs), such as high-temperature strength, high hardness, and good phase stability at high temperatures [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] , [7] ]. They are mainly composed of Mo, Nb, Ta, and W, while Ti, Cr, V, Si, and Al are usually used as strengthening alloy elements [ [8] , [9] , [10] , [11] , [12] , [13] , [14] ]. For example, Mo 25 Nb 25 Ta 25 W 25 and Mo 20 Nb 20 Ta 20 W 20 V 20 are two of the types of most extensively studied RHEAs [ [7] ]. The neutron diffraction analysis of those alloys after annealing at 1400 °C for 19 h shows that no changes have occurred to their phase structures. Their compression yield strengths are much higher than that of Inconel 718 alloy at temperatures above 800 °C. Furthermore, their yield strengths are still higher than 500 MPa at 1200 °C [ [15] , [16] ].
